title: Your first monthly budget
blurb: Ravi earns {income} a month. Split it into jars, deal with the leftover, and plan for good and lean months.
t1.title: Your plan for the month
t1.hook: Ravi earns {income} a month helping at his uncle's kirana shop. On the first day he splits the money into three jars: needs, wants and saving.
t1.define: A **budget** is a plan for your money, made before you spend it. It gives each rupee a job.
t1.analogy: Picture three jars on a shelf: needs, wants and saving. Each rupee goes into a jar on day one, so you always know what a jar is for.
q1.hint: Think about when a budget is made: before or after spending?
q1.explain: A budget gives each rupee a job before you spend it. It can include fun.
q1.opt.a: A plan that gives each rupee a job before you spend it
q1.opt.b: A list of everything you are not allowed to buy
q1.fb.b: A budget is not a ban on fun. It can include a wants jar, so fun is planned, not forbidden.
q1.opt.c: A record of what you spent last year
q2.prompt: Ravi puts {needsShare} of {income} into the needs jar. How many rupees is that? Type a number.
t2.title: Shares, not rules
t2.define: A **share** is a part of your income. A rule like 50/30/20 splits it into needs, wants and saving. It is one example, not a law.
t2.steps.3: Saving jar = income × saving share, set aside first
q3.prompt: Ravi gives wants a share of {wantsShare}. How many rupees go into the wants jar? Type a number.
q4.prompt: Meena's rent and bills take {rentShare} of her income. The 50/30/20 split does not fit her. What is a sensible move?
q4.hint: A share rule is a starting point.
q4.explain: Change the shares to fit your real life, and keep some saving, even if it is small.
q4.opt.a: Copy the rule anyway and borrow the gap
q4.fb.a: A share rule is an example. If your needs are bigger, change the shares to fit your real life.
q4.opt.b: Change the shares to fit her life, and still keep some saving
q4.opt.c: Stop saving, since needs are too big
q4.fb.c: Saving only what is left over often means saving nothing. A small saving share, set aside first, builds the habit.
t3.title: The leftover
t3.note: Say Ravi spends less than his wants jar. What remains is the **leftover**. It is not free money. It still needs a job.
q5.prompt: Ravi's wants jar holds {wantsAmt}. He spent {wantsSpent} of it. How much is left in the jar? Type a number.
q5.hint: Jar amount minus what he spent.
q6.prompt: What is a good thing to do with the leftover?
q6.hint: Money without a job tends to disappear.
q6.explain: Give the leftover a job on purpose: add it to saving, or carry it into next month.
q6.opt.a: Spend it, it is free money
q6.fb.a: Leftover is not free money. It is part of your plan, so give it a job before it vanishes.
q6.opt.b: Give it a job: add it to saving or carry it to next month
t4.title: A good month and a lean month
t4.define: Some people earn a different amount each month: a farmer, a tutor, a shop helper. They need a plan that survives a lean month.
t4.explore: Open the lab. Change the income to see a good month and a lean month. Try changing the shares too.
q7.prompt: A lean month: Ravi earns {leanMonth} and keeps a saving share of {saveShare}. How much goes into saving? Type a number.
q7.hint: Multiply {leanMonth} by {saveShare}. The lab can check it.
q8.prompt: Ravi earns {goodMonth} in a good month and {leanMonth} in a lean month. Which way of planning is safest?
q8.hint: Think about which month is harder to survive.
q8.explain: Plan the jars around the lean month, and put the extra from good months to use later.
q8.opt.a: Spend all of the good month, since he earned it
q8.fb.a: A good month does not repeat on its own. Spending it all leaves nothing for the lean month.
q8.opt.b: Plan around the lean month, and save the extra from good months
q8.opt.c: Plan only for the good month
q8.opt.d: Do not plan, the months vary
t5.title: The once-a-year cost
t5.misconception: Many people leave out costs that come once a year, like festivals, school fees or a phone repair. Then one month blows up. A budget needs a small monthly set-aside for them.
t5.steps.1: Find the yearly cost: Diwali gifts and sweets, {festival}
t5.steps.2: Divide it by the months in a year
t5.steps.3: Put that much aside every month
q9.prompt: Diwali costs Ravi {festival} once a year. How much should he set aside each month? Type a number.
q9.hint: Divide {festival} by the months in a year.
q9.explain: {festival} divided by 12 months is {festMonthly} a month.
q10.prompt: It is August and Ravi has set nothing aside for Diwali. What fits this lesson best?
q10.hint: A small start is better than none.
q10.explain: Start a small monthly set-aside now. Even a part of the full amount helps.
q10.opt.a: Skip it, once a year does not count
q10.fb.a: A yearly cost still has to be paid. Leaving it out of the budget just moves the shock to one month.
q10.opt.b: Start a small monthly set-aside now
q10.opt.c: Borrow from a friend in October and forget it
glossary.plan_budget.def: A plan that gives every rupee a job before you spend it.
glossary.plan_income.def: Money that comes in, such as pay or pocket money.
glossary.plan_share.def: A part of your income, often written as a percentage.
glossary.plan_leftover.def: Money still unspent in a jar at the end of the month.
